blocks.text: Imagine trying to test a new software application without a systematic approach—how would you ensure that all critical functionalities are checked?

blocks.markdown: In software engineering, designing effective test cases is crucial for ensuring the quality and reliability of software systems. This lesson will introduce you to key techniques such as equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, and coverage criteria. We'll also explore the use of test doubles like mocks and stubs to isolate units under test.

blocks.title: Equivalence Partitioning
blocks.text: Equivalence partitioning is a testing technique that divides input data into partitions of equivalent data from which test cases can be derived.

blocks.markdown: The idea behind equivalence partitioning is to reduce the number of test cases by identifying inputs that are expected to produce similar behavior. Each partition represents a set of inputs that should be treated the same by the system.

blocks.title: Boundary Value Analysis
blocks.text: Boundary value analysis focuses on testing the boundaries between partitions. It is based on the observation that errors often occur at the edges of input ranges.

blocks.title: Equivalence Partitioning Example
blocks.prompt: Consider a function that accepts an integer input representing age and determines if a person is eligible to vote (age >= 18). Derive test cases using equivalence partitioning.

steps.text: Identify the partitions for the input domain. Here, we have two partitions: ages less than 18 and ages 18 or older.
Select representative values from each partition. For ages less than 18, choose a value like 17. For ages 18 or older, choose a value like 18.
Create test cases using these representative values. Test with age = 17 (expect false) and age = 18 (expect true).

blocks.answer: Test cases: (1) age = 17, expect false; (2) age = 18, expect true.

blocks.title: Boundary Value Analysis Example
blocks.prompt: Using the same voting eligibility function, derive test cases using boundary value analysis.

steps.text: Identify the boundary values. For this function, the critical boundary is at age 18.
Test just below, at, and just above the boundary. Choose ages 17, 18, and 19.
Create test cases: age = 17 (expect false), age = 18 (expect true), age = 19 (expect true).

blocks.answer: Test cases: (1) age = 17, expect false; (2) age = 18, expect true; (3) age = 19, expect true.

blocks.title: Coverage Criteria
blocks.text: Statement coverage ensures each line of code is executed at least once, while branch coverage ensures each branch of decision points is executed.

blocks.markdown: Coverage criteria help in assessing the thoroughness of test cases. However, achieving 100% coverage does not guarantee the absence of defects.

blocks.markdown: In practice, achieving full coverage can be challenging and may not always be cost-effective. It's essential to balance coverage goals with practical constraints.

blocks.title: Test Doubles
blocks.text: Test doubles are objects that mimic the behavior of real components. Mocks and stubs are common types of test doubles used to isolate units under test.

blocks.markdown: Mocks are used to verify interactions between objects, while stubs provide predefined responses to method calls. Both help in isolating the unit under test from its dependencies.

points: Equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis are effective techniques for deriving test cases.
Statement and branch coverage help assess test thoroughness but do not guarantee defect-free software.
Test doubles like mocks and stubs are useful for isolating units under test.
